# Soft Polyurethane Foam Molded Article

## Technical Field

The present invention relates to a soft polyurethane foam molded article (1) having a mounting surface (1A), which is formed through a foam-molding process using a foaming stock solution. This invention addresses the structural characteristics of the foam cells within the molded article and their distribution pattern throughout the material's thickness.

## Structural Configuration

The molded article is characterized by a multi-layered structure comprising a plurality of distinct layered parts, specifically identified as layered part (11) and layered part (12). These layered parts are formed and arranged so as to create clearly distinguishable layers extending in a vertical direction (Y), wherein this vertical direction is defined as being perpendicular to the mounting surface (1A) of the molded article. This layered configuration results from the foam-molding process and reflects variations in the internal cellular structure that occur as a function of position within the foam body.

## Cell Geometry Within Individual Layers

Within each individual layered part, the foaming cells present in the foam structure exhibit a characteristic geometric property: the ratio of the lateral (horizontal) size of the cells to their vertical size increases progressively as the cells are positioned closer to the mounting surface (1A). In other words, within any given layer, cells located nearer to the mounting surface tend to be relatively more elongated or flattened in the lateral direction relative to their vertical dimension, whereas cells located farther from the mounting surface within that same layer exhibit a comparatively lower lateral-to-vertical size ratio. This gradient in cell geometry occurs continuously within each layered part.

## Cell Ratio Relationship at Layer Boundaries

A distinguishing structural feature of the present invention is found at the boundaries between adjacent layered parts, specifically at boundary regions denoted as (C1) and (A2). At these boundaries, a discontinuity in the cell ratio trend is observed: the foaming cell ratio in the layered part positioned nearer to the mounting surface (11) is lower than the corresponding foaming cell ratio found in the layered part positioned nearer to the back surface (12). This means that, rather than the lateral-to-vertical cell size ratio increasing monotonically and continuously throughout the entire thickness of the molded article, there is instead a discrete step-change or discontinuity at the interface between the two layered parts, wherein the cell ratio effectively resets to a lower value in the layer closer to the mounting surface as compared to the cell ratio present in the adjoining layer closer to the back surface.

## Definition of the Back Surface and Structural Contrast

The back surface (1B) of the molded article is defined as the surface located on the side opposite to the mounting surface (1A). This definition establishes a clear structural framework within which the two layered parts (11) and (12) can be understood as occupying distinguishable positions relative to the two opposing surfaces of the molded article. As a result of the cell ratio relationship described above, a structural contrast is established between the layered part associated with the mounting surface and the layered part associated with the back surface, in terms of their respective foaming cell geometries. This contrast in cell structure between the two layers contributes to the distinctive mechanical and physical properties of the molded article as a whole, differentiating it from conventional soft polyurethane foam products that may exhibit a more uniform or continuously graded cellular structure throughout their thickness.

# Soft Polyurethane Foam Molded Article with Layered Cell Structure

## Field of the Invention

This invention relates to a soft polyurethane foam molded article, particularly one designed for applications requiring optimized comfort and mechanical performance characteristics, such as seating cushions, bedding products, and other load-bearing foam applications where the interaction between the mounting surface (the surface in contact with a supporting structure or seated user) and the back surface (the opposite, typically unseen surface) plays a critical role in overall product performance.

## Background and Technical Problem

Conventional soft polyurethane foam articles are typically manufactured as homogeneous structures with relatively uniform cellular architecture throughout their thickness. While such uniform structures are straightforward to manufacture, they often fail to provide the optimal balance of properties needed for different regions of the foam. Specifically, the surface intended for direct contact with a user (the mounting surface) has different mechanical requirements than the surface facing away from the user (the back surface). A single uniform foam structure represents a compromise that may sacrifice comfort at the mounting surface or structural support at the back surface, or both.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention addresses these limitations by providing a soft polyurethane foam molded article structured as multiple vertically layered parts formed from a foaming stock solution. Rather than producing a single homogeneous foam body, the invention deliberately creates a laminar structure in which each layer possesses distinct cellular characteristics tailored to its position within the overall thickness of the article.

### Layer Structure and Cell Geometry

Each of the vertically stacked layers is characterized by foaming cells whose lateral-to-vertical size ratio (i.e., the ratio between the cell dimension measured in the horizontal or lateral direction and the cell dimension measured in the vertical direction) is not constant throughout the article. Instead, this ratio is configured to increase progressively as the layers approach the mounting surface. In other words, cells located closer to the surface that will bear direct contact with a user or supporting structure are relatively more elongated or flattened in the lateral direction relative to their vertical extent, as compared to cells located toward the back surface.

This gradient in cell geometry is achieved by controlling the foaming and curing conditions during the formation of each layer from the foaming stock solution, allowing manufacturers to engineer a foam body with continuously or stepwise varying cellular characteristics without requiring discrete, separately manufactured foam pieces to be bonded together after the fact.

### Boundary Cell Ratio Relationship

A key structural feature of the invention concerns the relationship between adjacent layers at their boundaries. At each boundary interface between two adjacent vertically stacked layers, the foaming cell ratio characteristic of the layer situated on the mounting-surface side of that boundary is deliberately set to be lower than the foaming cell ratio characteristic of the layer situated on the back-surface side of that same boundary.

This means that, at every layer-to-layer transition within the foam structure, there exists a discontinuity or step-change in cell ratio, with the mounting-surface-side layer at that boundary always exhibiting a comparatively lower lateral-to-vertical cell ratio than the back-surface-side layer immediately adjacent to it. This relationship holds true at each and every boundary throughout the multi-layered structure, creating a systematic and repeatable pattern of controlled discontinuities superimposed on the overall gradient described above.

## Technical Significance

This carefully engineered structural configuration—combining an overall increasing trend in cell ratio toward the mounting surface with deliberately lowered cell ratios at the mounting-surface side of each layer boundary—has been found to be significant for optimizing the mechanical and comfort properties of the resulting foam article.

The layered approach with controlled boundary discontinuities allows the foam to achieve several performance objectives simultaneously:

1. **Localized Comfort Optimization**: By managing cell geometry near the mounting surface with lower ratios at boundary regions, the invention can provide a more compliant, comfortable initial response to loading at the surface most directly experienced by a user.

2. **Progressive Support Characteristics**: The overall increase in cell ratio toward the mounting surface, combined with the boundary effects, allows the foam to exhibit progressive firmness characteristics as compression increases, providing initial softness with increasing support as load increases.

3. **Structural Integration**: Because the layers are formed from a common foaming stock solution rather than being manufactured separately and joined, the resulting article maintains structural integrity across layer boundaries while still achieving the desired property gradients, avoiding potential weaknesses or delamination issues associated with adhesively bonded multi-component foam structures.

4. **Tunable Mechanical Response**: The specific relationship between cell ratios at each boundary provides manufacturers with an additional design parameter—beyond simple density or overall cell size control—for fine-tuning the mechanical response of the foam article to match specific application requirements.

## Conclusion

By providing a soft polyurethane foam molded article with this specifically engineered multi-layer cellular architecture—featuring both an overall gradient in lateral-to-vertical cell ratio toward the mounting surface and controlled, deliberately lowered cell ratios at the mounting-surface side of each inter-layer boundary—this invention offers a technically sophisticated solution for producing foam products with superior, tailored combinations of mechanical performance and user comfort, applicable across a range of foam product applications where such optimized layered performance is desired.

# The Definite Article: A Small Word with Outsized Power

At just three letters long, "the" holds the title of the most frequently used word in the English language. It appears in roughly 5-7% of all words in typical English text—more often than any other word, including common companions like "and," "of," or "to."

## What Makes "The" So Essential?

"The" is a definite article, a small but mighty grammatical tool that transforms vague nouns into specific ones. Compare "I saw a dog" with "I saw the dog." The first sentence introduces any dog, an unknown creature wandering into the narrative. The second sentence implies a particular dog—one already known to speaker and listener, perhaps mentioned earlier or understood from context.

This distinction between definite and indefinite reference is crucial to how English speakers communicate precisely. Without "the," we'd lose an entire layer of meaning that helps listeners track what's being discussed.

## A Word Many Languages Lack

Interestingly, not all languages have articles at all. Russian, Japanese, and Mandarin Chinese, for example, get along fine without them, relying instead on context, word order, or other grammatical markers to convey definiteness. This is why native speakers of these languages often find English articles (`a`, `an`, `the`) among the trickiest aspects of English grammar to master—there's no direct equivalent to translate.

## The Word's Ancient Roots

"The" descends from Old English demonstrative pronouns like "sē," "sēo," and "þæt," which meant "that" or "this." Over centuries, these forms gradually simplified and merged into the single, gender-neutral "the" we use today—a linguistic evolution reflecting English's broader shift away from complex grammatical gender systems.

## Conclusion

Though easy to overlook, "the" plays an outsized role in clarity and meaning. It's a reminder that even the smallest words can carry significant grammatical weight, shaping how we understand and communicate about the world around us.

# ABSTRACT

A soft polyurethane foam molded article is disclosed having a layered foaming cell structure that provides enhanced cushioning properties and structural stability while maintaining a lightweight profile suitable for seating, bedding, and related cushioning applications.

The molded article (1) comprises a mounting surface (10) configured to support or interface with an external structural member, and a foam body formed integrally therewith through a molding process that produces a plurality of distinct cellular layers arranged in a stacked configuration extending from the mounting surface (10) toward an opposing upper surface of the article.

The foam body includes a first layer (21) disposed adjacent to and in contact with the mounting surface (10), the first layer (21) characterized by a first average cell size and a first density suited to providing a firm supportive base. A second layer (22) is disposed above the first layer (21) and exhibits a second average cell size different from the first average cell size, the second layer (22) providing an intermediate cushioning characteristic. A third layer (23) is disposed above the second layer (22), forming an uppermost or outer layer of the foam body, the third layer (23) exhibiting a third average cell size different from both the first and second average cell sizes, thereby providing a softer surface-contact cushioning characteristic relative to the underlying layers.

A first boundary (31) is defined at the interface between the first layer (21) and the second layer (22), the first boundary (31) representing a transitional zone in which cell size and density gradually or discretely change between the two adjacent layers. A second boundary (32) is defined at the interface between the second layer (22) and the third layer (23), the second boundary (32) similarly representing a transitional zone between the differing cellular structures of the second layer (22) and third layer (23).

The layered foaming cell structure is achieved through a controlled foam-rise molding technique in which foaming reactants are introduced into a mold cavity under conditions promoting differential cell nucleation and growth rates across the vertical extent of the mold, resulting in the formation of the first layer (21), second layer (22), and third layer (23) with their respective boundaries (31, 32) in a single integrated molding operation, without requiring separate adhesive bonding or lamination of discrete foam sheets.

The resulting molded article (1) exhibits a gradient of mechanical properties—including hardness, resilience, and air permeability—progressing from the mounting surface (10) through the first layer (21), first boundary (31), second layer (22), second boundary (32), and third layer (23), thereby achieving a cushioning performance that combines firm structural support near the mounting surface (10) with progressively softer, more conforming comfort characteristics at the outer surface of the article, while maintaining structural integrity across the boundaries (31, 32) due to the continuous, integrally molded nature of the foam body.

This construction enables manufacture of a cushioning article with tailored multi-zone comfort and support characteristics in a single molding step, reducing production complexity and material waste associated with conventional multi-layer foam lamination methods, while improving durability at the layer interfaces through the elimination of discrete bonding lines.

# Multilayer Polyurethane Foam Article with Graduated Cell Elongation Ratios

## Detailed Description

Referring generally to the figures, a multilayer polyurethane foam part (1) is provided, comprising at least a first foam layer (1A) and a second foam layer (1B) disposed in contacting relation along an interfacial boundary region, wherein the cellular morphology of said layers exhibits a differential cell elongation ratio across the thickness dimension of the multilayer foam part (1).

The first foam layer (1A) comprises a first plurality of foam cells (11) having a first average cell elongation ratio, said first average cell elongation ratio being defined as the ratio of the major axis dimension to the minor axis dimension of a representative sampling of said foam cells (11), measured in a cross-sectional plane substantially parallel to the rise direction of the foam during formation thereof.

The second foam layer (1B) comprises a second plurality of foam cells (12) having a second average cell elongation ratio, wherein said second average cell elongation ratio differs from said first average cell elongation ratio by a predetermined margin, said margin being selected to impart differential mechanical properties—including but not limited to compression set resistance, tensile strength, and anisotropic load-bearing characteristics—across the multilayer foam part (1).

In certain embodiments, the first average cell elongation ratio of foam cells (11) within first foam layer (1A) ranges from about 1.0:1 to about 1.8:1, whereas the second average cell elongation ratio of foam cells (12) within second foam layer (1B) ranges from about 1.8:1 to about 3.5:1, such that a gradient transition in cell morphology is established proceeding from first foam layer (1A) toward second foam layer (1B).

A first core sample (C1), extracted from a central region of first foam layer (1A) via a coring tool oriented perpendicular to the layer boundary, exhibits a first measured cell elongation ratio substantially consistent with said first average cell elongation ratio. Correspondingly, a second core sample, extractable from second foam layer (1B) in like manner, exhibits a second measured cell elongation ratio substantially consistent with said second average cell elongation ratio, thereby confirming the graduated cellular structure across the thickness of multilayer foam part (1).

The multilayer foam part (1) may further comprise an additional foam layer (A2) disposed adjacent to, or interposed between, first foam layer (1A) and second foam layer (1B), said additional foam layer (A2) comprising a third plurality of foam cells having a third average cell elongation ratio intermediate between said first average cell elongation ratio and said second average cell elongation ratio, thereby providing a stepped or continuous gradient in cell elongation ratio across the multilayer foam part (1).

In some embodiments, the differential cell elongation ratio between first foam layer (1A) and second foam layer (1B) is achieved through control of one or more processing parameters selected from the group consisting of: (i) differential foaming reaction temperatures applied to respective precursor layers; (ii) differential catalyst concentrations incorporated into respective foam-forming compositions; (iii) differential mold cavity geometries constraining the rise direction of respective foam layers; (iv) mechanical compression applied to at least one of said foam layers during or after curing; and (v) differential blowing agent concentrations incorporated into respective foam-forming compositions.

It is contemplated that the cell elongation ratio gradient extending from foam cells (11) of first foam layer (1A) to foam cells (12) of second foam layer (1B) may be substantially linear, stepwise, exponential, or otherwise non-uniform, depending upon the intended end-use application and desired anisotropic performance characteristics of the multilayer foam part (1).

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates to a soft foam product having a plurality of foaming cells distributed in a layered configuration, wherein the geometric characteristics of the foaming cells vary progressively across the thickness of the product to achieve enhanced comfort, support, and durability characteristics.

In one aspect, the soft foam product comprises a foam body having a top surface and a bottom surface opposing the top surface, with the foam body defining a thickness direction extending between the top surface and the bottom surface. The foam body includes a first region, a second region, and a third region arranged sequentially along the thickness direction, wherein the first region is disposed proximate the top surface, the third region is disposed proximate the bottom surface, and the second region is disposed intermediate the first region and the third region. A first boundary is defined between the first region and the second region, and a second boundary is defined between the second region and the third region.

Each of the first region, the second region, and the third region includes a plurality of foaming cells, each foaming cell having a lateral dimension measured substantially perpendicular to the thickness direction and a vertical dimension measured substantially parallel to the thickness direction. Each foaming cell is characterized by a lateral-to-vertical size ratio calculated as the lateral dimension divided by the vertical dimension.

According to the invention, the lateral-to-vertical size ratio of the foaming cells changes progressively from the first region, through the second region, to the third region. In one embodiment, the foaming cells in the first region proximate the top surface exhibit a first average lateral-to-vertical size ratio, the foaming cells in the second region exhibit a second average lateral-to-vertical size ratio, and the foaming cells in the third region proximate the bottom surface exhibit a third average lateral-to-vertical size ratio, wherein the first average lateral-to-vertical size ratio is greater than the second average lateral-to-vertical size ratio, and the second average lateral-to-vertical size ratio is greater than the third average lateral-to-vertical size ratio. In this configuration, the foaming cells transition from a relatively flattened, laterally elongated geometry near the top surface to a relatively elongated, vertically oriented geometry near the bottom surface, with the first boundary and the second boundary representing transitional zones rather than abrupt discontinuities, such that the change in cell geometry occurs in a substantially continuous or gradient manner across the first boundary and the second boundary.

In some embodiments, the progressive change in the lateral-to-vertical size ratio is achieved through controlled variation of foaming parameters during manufacture, including but not limited to temperature gradients, pressure gradients, blowing agent concentration gradients, or curing rate gradients applied across the thickness of the foam body during a foaming process. In other embodiments, the foam body is formed by sequentially depositing or curing multiple foam layers corresponding to the first region, the second region, and the third region, wherein each layer is formulated or processed to yield foaming cells having the desired average lateral-to-vertical size ratio, and wherein the first boundary and the second boundary correspond to interfaces between adjacent layers that are subsequently blended, fused, or otherwise processed to minimize mechanical discontinuity.

The progressive variation in foaming cell geometry across the first region, the second region, and the third region enables the soft foam product to exhibit a gradient of mechanical properties through its thickness. For example, the relatively flattened foaming cells proximate the top surface may provide increased surface conformability and a softer initial compression response, while the relatively elongated foaming cells proximate the bottom surface may provide increased resistance to compression and enhanced structural support. The intermediate second region, having foaming cells with an intermediate lateral-to-vertical size ratio, provides a transitional mechanical response between the first region and the third region, thereby reducing the likelihood of an abrupt change in feel or support when the foam product is compressed, such as during use as a cushioning material, mattress core, seating pad, or similar application.

In further embodiments, additional regions beyond the first region, the second region, and the third region may be included, each having a corresponding average lateral-to-vertical size ratio, such that the foam body comprises four or more regions arranged along the thickness direction with progressively changing foaming cell geometry from the top surface to the bottom surface. Additionally, the rate of change of the lateral-to-vertical size ratio between adjacent regions may itself vary, such that the transition proximate the first boundary differs from the transition proximate the second boundary, allowing for customizable comfort and support profiles tailored to particular applications.

It is to be understood that both the foregoing general description and the following detailed description are exemplary and explanatory only and are not restrictive of the invention as claimed.
